Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Amir was forty years old, a paramedic for over fifteen years, married with two children, and he had always thought of himself as someone who kept his head when others lost theirs. That ended on a Tuesday evening in late October, during a call that began as a routine response to a reported stabbing in a convenience store parking lot. His partner, Elena, was two years younger than him, quick-witted and steady, and they had worked together long enough to read each other’s movements without words. When they arrived, the scene was chaotic—a young man bleeding from a femoral wound, a woman screaming, bystanders filming on their phones. Amir knelt to apply pressure while Elena radioed for backup and began directing traffic. He did not see the second assailant emerge from behind the dumpster. He only heard the sound—a wet, hard crack—and then Elena was on the ground, her skull fractured by a steel pipe. He stayed with her, tried to stop the bleeding from her ear, but she was gone before the helicopter landed. In the weeks that followed, Amir could not stop replaying that moment: the sound, the way her eyes went blank, the warmth of her blood on his gloves. But there were gaps too—whole seconds he could not account for, like the time between hearing the crack and finding himself kneeling beside her. He had tried to fill them in, but the effort only made the memories that did come back feel more vivid, more real, until remembering her face brought the same cold terror he had felt in that parking lot.

At first, Amir went back to work the next week. It seemed like the right thing to do—the only thing he knew how to do. But soon the work itself became a trap. Every visible injury, every wound he dressed or tourniquet he applied, was Elena’s wound. Every victim he tried to calm was her. The antiseptic smell of the hospital emergency bay—sharp and chemical—hit him like a physical blow, flooding his sinuses with the memory of the helicopter’s interior and the futile resuscitation. He began to dread his shifts, but he could not bring himself to call in sick. Instead, he worked longer hours, took extra shifts, volunteered for the busiest stations. He told himself he was being dedicated, but the real reason was simpler: as long as he was running from call to call, he did not have time to think. The moment he stopped—sitting in the crew room, driving home in silence—the thoughts would rush in, and he would force them back down, clenching his jaw until his temples ached. He had come to believe that if he let himself remember fully, he would never be able to function again. So he suppressed, and he worked, and he suppressed again.

But the avoidance bled into everything. He stopped attending the monthly training sessions at the firehouse because the classroom smelled like the hospital. He started sitting with his back to the wall in every room—at the station, at home, even in his own living room. If his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he would flinch so hard he sometimes knocked her hand away. Concentration became a daily struggle: he would lose track of conversations mid-sentence, forget to eat lunch, drive past his exit on the way home. His wife noticed he was distant, irritable, and often wakeful; she assumed it was grief, and it was, but it was also something more tangled. Amir felt he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who used to joke with his crew and sleep through the night was gone. Worse, he had begun to believe that he could not rely on himself any longer. If he had been more alert, if he had scanned the parking lot better, he could have seen the second man. He should have protected Elena. She was his partner, his responsibility, and he had failed. The thought sat in his chest like a stone, and no amount of overtime could dislodge it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a shift three weeks ago. He was assigned to a call for an elderly man who had fallen and gashed his forehead. The wound was minor, but when Amir leaned in to clean it, the sight of the torn skin, the hospital antiseptic smell from the man’s own bathroom, and the memory of Elena’s head all fused into one seamless, horrifying moment. He could not move. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, the room dissolving around him until a colleague touched his arm and he yelped, stumbling backward. After that, his supervisor gently suggested he take time off. At home, alone with the silence, Amir finally admitted he could not keep going this way. He is afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that fully remembering will destroy him, or that he will discover he was never the man he thought he was. But he is also hoping, quietly, that there might be a way to live without the terror, without the constant watchfulness, without feeling that he has already failed everyone who matters.

missing_explanations: The vignette does not show the patient avoiding going to work or study; instead, he overworks by taking extra shifts and working longer hours.
